question: A patient with pulmonary tuberculosis has granulomas on lung biopsy. Which T-helper cell subset and its signature cytokine are primarily responsible for granuloma formation and macrophage activation in tuberculosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Th1 cells, driven by IL-12 from antigen-presenting cells, produce IFN-γ — the most potent macrophage-activating cytokine. Activated macrophages fuse into epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells, forming the granuloma that walls off M. tuberculosis. This Th1-driven cell-mediated immunity is the principal defence against intracellular pathogens.

Incorrect. Th2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, driving B cell class switching to IgE, eosinophil recruitment, and mucus production — the response against helminths and in allergic disease. Granuloma formation in TB depends on Th1 cells and IFN-γ-mediated macrophage activation.

Incorrect. Th17 cells produce IL-17 and are important for mucosal defence against extracellular bacteria and fungi (especially Candida). While Th17 cells contribute to some inflammatory responses, granuloma formation in TB is predominantly Th1-mediated via IFN-γ-driven macrophage activation.

Incorrect. Treg cells produce TGF-β and IL-10 to suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance. They counterbalance effector responses but do not drive granuloma formation. TB granulomas depend on Th1 cells producing IFN-γ to activate macrophages into epithelioid and giant cells.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Th cell subsets: Th1 (IFN-γ, macrophage activation, intracellular pathogens), Th2 (IL-4, IgE, helminths), Th17 (IL-17, mucosal fungi/bacteria), Treg (TGF-β, immune suppression).
Well done! The Th1–IFN-γ–macrophage activation axis is the cornerstone of antimycobacterial immunity and granuloma formation.
